q: An 'investment centre' is a responsibility centre whose manager is accountable for:

options.D: Revenues, costs and the capital invested in the centre, performance being measured through return on investment

e: An investment centre's manager is accountable for revenues, costs and the capital invested in the centre, performance being measured through return on investment.

q: Which of the following is classified as an investing activity in a cash flow statement?

options.D: Repayment of a bank loan

e: Purchase of machinery is an investing activity (cash outflow for a long-term asset); issue of share capital and loan repayment are financing activities, and wages are an operating activity.

q: Performance budgeting primarily seeks to relate:

options.A: Expenditure to the previous year's actuals
options.B: Inputs to the number of staff employed
options.C: Financial outlays to physical targets and programme outputs
options.D: Revenue expenditure to capital expenditure

e: Performance budgeting relates financial outlays to physical targets and programme outputs, so that expenditure is judged by the results achieved rather than only by amounts spent.

q: Under responsibility accounting, a manager should be held accountable only for:

options.A: All the costs of the enterprise
options.B: The costs and revenues over which he can exercise significant control
options.C: Costs recorded in the general books of account
options.D: Fixed costs of his department only

e: Under responsibility accounting, a manager is held accountable only for the costs and revenues over which he can exercise significant control (the controllability principle).

q: 'Permanent' (core) working capital refers to:

options.A: The working capital required to meet seasonal peaks of activity
options.B: The amount of working capital borrowed from banks on a continuing basis
options.C: Current assets financed wholly by long-term loans
options.D: The minimum level of working capital that must be maintained throughout the year for carrying on operations

e: Permanent (core) working capital is the minimum level of working capital that must be maintained throughout the year for carrying on operations; seasonal peaks require additional temporary working capital.

q: Differential cost is best described as:

options.A: A past cost that cannot be recovered
options.B: The difference in total cost between two alternative courses of action
options.C: The cost that remains unchanged between alternatives
options.D: The benefit forgone from the next best alternative

e: Differential cost is the difference in total cost between two alternative courses of action; only such differing costs (and revenues) are relevant in choosing between alternatives.

q: The cash break-even point is the level of sales at which the total contribution is exactly equal to:

options.B: Cash inflows from all sources for the year
options.C: Only the cash fixed costs, non-cash items such as depreciation being excluded
options.D: The profit after tax of the enterprise

e: At the cash break-even point, total contribution exactly equals only the cash fixed costs; non-cash items such as depreciation are excluded because they involve no cash outgo.

q: A high degree of operating leverage in an enterprise indicates that:

options.A: A small change in sales volume will bring about a relatively large change in operating profit
options.B: Fixed costs are negligible in its cost structure
options.C: Its profits are almost insensitive to changes in sales
options.D: It carries no business risk at all

e: A high degree of operating leverage (a large proportion of fixed costs) means a small change in sales volume brings about a relatively large change in operating profit.

q: When the output of a factory is restricted by a limiting (key) factor, the relative profitability of the products is judged by:

options.A: Contribution per unit of the product
options.B: Net profit per unit of the product
options.C: Contribution per unit of the limiting factor
options.D: Sales value per unit of the product

e: When a limiting (key) factor restricts output, products are ranked by contribution per unit of the limiting factor, so that the scarce resource earns the maximum total contribution.

q: A product sells for Rs 120 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 84 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 1,80,000. The break-even point in units is:

options.D: 15,000 units

e: Contribution per unit = 120 - 84 = Rs 36; Break-even point = 1,80,000 / 36 = 5,000 units.

q: Fixed costs are Rs 2,40,000 and the P/V ratio is 40%. The sales required to earn a profit of Rs 80,000 are:
e: Sales for desired profit = (Fixed cost + Desired profit) / P/V ratio = (2,40,000 + 80,000) / 0.40 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: Sales are Rs 20,00,000, variable costs are Rs 14,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Contribution = 20,00,000 - 14,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000; Operating profit = 6,00,000 - 2,00,000 = Rs 4,00,000; Degree of operating leverage = Contribution / Operating profit = 6,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 1.5.

q: A firm sells two products. Product A has sales of Rs 4,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 50%, and Product B has sales of Rs 6,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 25%. Total fixed costs are Rs 3,50,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:

Products X and Y are made on the same machine, whose hours are the limiting factor. X gives a contribution of Rs 60 per unit and takes 2 machine-hours per unit; Y gives a contribution of Rs 100 per unit and takes 4 machine-hours per unit. To maximise profit, production priority should be given to:

options.A: Y, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Y, because it uses more machine-hours per unit
options.D: X, because its contribution per machine-hour is higher

e: Contribution per machine-hour: X = 60 / 2 = Rs 30, Y = 100 / 4 = Rs 25. Machine-hours being the limiting factor, X earns more per scarce hour and gets production priority.

q: A firm has spare capacity. Its regular selling price is Rs 100 per unit and the variable cost is Rs 65 per unit. It receives a one-time export order for 2,000 units at Rs 75 per unit, involving no extra fixed cost. The order should be:

options.A: Accepted only if the price covers the total cost per unit
options.B: Rejected, because the price is below the regular selling price
options.C: Accepted, because the price exceeds the variable cost and the order adds Rs 20,000 to profit
options.D: Rejected, because it will reduce the margin of safety

e: With spare capacity and no extra fixed cost, only the variable cost of Rs 65 is incremental; the price of Rs 75 gives Rs 10 extra contribution per unit, adding 2,000 x 10 = Rs 20,000 to profit, so the order should be accepted.

q: A component can be made in-house at a variable cost of Rs 36 per unit (materials Rs 18, labour Rs 12, variable overheads Rs 6). An outside supplier offers it at Rs 40 per unit. Allocated fixed overheads of Rs 5 per unit will continue whether the component is made or bought. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make, because the relevant cost of making (Rs 36) is less than the purchase price (Rs 40)
options.B: Buy, because the total in-house cost of Rs 41 exceeds the supplier's price
options.C: Buy, because the fixed overheads will then be saved
options.D: Remain indifferent, the costs being equal

e: The allocated fixed overheads of Rs 5 continue whether the component is made or bought and are irrelevant; the relevant cost of making (Rs 36) is less than the purchase price (Rs 40), so it should be made.

q: A special job requires material which the firm already holds in stock, purchased earlier at Rs 40 per kg. The material is in regular use in the factory and its current replacement price is Rs 55 per kg. The relevant cost of the material for pricing this job is:

options.B: Nil, since the material is already in stock
options.C: Rs 47.50 per kg, being the average of the two prices
options.D: Rs 55 per kg

e: The material is in regular use, so consuming it on this job requires its replacement; the relevant cost is therefore the current replacement price of Rs 55 per kg, not the sunk historic price.

q: In the short run, it is worthwhile continuing a product line so long as:

options.A: Its contribution exceeds the fixed costs that would be avoided if it were discontinued
options.B: It recovers its full allocated cost including common overheads
options.C: It earns a positive accounting profit after all allocations
options.D: Its sales are higher than those of every other product line

e: In the short run, a product line is worth continuing so long as its contribution exceeds the fixed costs that would actually be avoided if it were discontinued; unavoidable common costs are irrelevant.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 25 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 27 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 2,000 kg. The material price variance is:

options.D: Rs 54,000 (Adverse)

e: Material price variance = (Standard price - Actual price) x Actual quantity = (25 - 27) x 2,000 = Rs 4,000 (Adverse), because a higher price was paid than standard.

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 60 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 58 per hour for 500 actual hours worked. The labour rate variance is:

options.D: Nil

e: Labour rate variance = (Standard rate - Actual rate) x Actual hours = (60 - 58) x 500 = Rs 1,000 (Favourable), because labour was paid at less than the standard rate.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 1,200 hours, but only 1,100 hours were actually taken. The standard rate is Rs 30 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:

options.D: Rs 3,600 (Favourable)

e: Labour efficiency variance = (Standard hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (1,200 - 1,100) x 30 = Rs 3,000 (Favourable), because the work took fewer hours than the standard allows.

q: The material mix variance arises when:

options.A: The actual price of material differs from the standard price
options.B: The proportion in which the different materials are actually mixed differs from the standard proportion
options.C: The total quantity of material used exceeds the standard quantity
options.D: The output obtained is less than the standard yield

e: Material mix variance arises when the proportion in which the different materials are actually mixed differs from the standard proportion; total quantity differences are covered by the yield variance.

q: The material yield variance measures:

options.A: The effect of changes in the price of materials on cost
options.B: The difference between the standard output (yield) expected from the actual input and the actual output obtained, valued at standard cost
options.C: Wastage of material in stores handling only
options.D: The difference between standard and actual wage cost

e: Material yield variance measures the difference between the standard output expected from the actual input and the actual output obtained, valued at the standard cost per unit of output.

q: Under 'management by exception' in variance reporting:

options.A: All variances, however small, are investigated in equal detail
options.B: Variances are reported but never investigated
options.C: Budgets themselves are prepared only in exceptional years
options.D: Only significant variances are reported to and investigated by management, so that attention is focused where control action is needed

e: Under management by exception, only significant variances are reported to and investigated by management, so that attention and control action are focused where they are most needed.

q: A budget for 10,000 units provides for fixed costs of Rs 2,00,000 and variable costs of Rs 30 per unit. The flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 8,000 units will be:
e: Flexed budget allowance = Fixed costs + Variable cost at actual output = 2,00,000 + 30 x 8,000 = Rs 4,40,000; fixed costs do not change with output.

q: In zero-base budgeting, a 'decision package' is:

options.A: A document in which a manager justifies an activity from the zero base, stating its cost, benefits and the consequences of not approving it, so that packages can be ranked in order of priority
options.B: The final budget as approved by the competent authority
options.C: A software package used for preparing budgets
options.D: A bundle of papers forwarded to the Railway Board for sanction

e: A decision package is the document in which a manager justifies an activity from the zero base, stating its cost, benefits and the consequences of not approving it, so packages can be ranked in priority order.

q: The 'principal budget factor' (key budget factor) is:

options.A: The factor which limits the activities of the enterprise and determines the order in which the functional budgets are prepared, e.g., sales demand
options.B: The largest single item of expenditure in the budget
options.C: The officer in charge of budget preparation
options.D: The cash budget, because it is prepared first

e: The principal budget factor is the factor that limits the activities of the enterprise (e.g., sales demand) and determines the order in which the functional budgets are prepared.

q: A rolling (continuous) budget is a budget which:

options.A: Is prepared once for the whole life of the enterprise
options.B: Is revised continuously by adding a budget for a further period and dropping the period just completed, so that it always covers a fixed forward period
options.C: Cannot be changed under any circumstances
options.D: Covers cash transactions only

e: A rolling (continuous) budget is revised continuously by adding a budget for a further period and dropping the period just completed, so that it always covers a fixed forward period.

q: A 'profit centre' is a responsibility centre whose manager is accountable for:

options.C: Capital expenditure of the centre only
options.D: Both the revenues and the costs of the centre, that is, its profit

e: A profit centre's manager is accountable for both the revenues and the costs of the centre, that is, for its profit; control over investment would make it an investment centre.

q: The main objectives of a sound transfer pricing system for inter-divisional transfers are to:

options.A: Maximise the tax liability of the enterprise
options.B: Promote goal congruence and preserve divisional autonomy, while enabling a fair measurement of divisional performance
options.D: Fix the selling price of the final product

e: A sound transfer pricing system should promote goal congruence (divisions acting in the company's overall interest) and preserve divisional autonomy, while enabling fair measurement of divisional performance.

q: Under the cost-plus method of transfer pricing, the transfer price is set at:

options.A: The market price of the product
options.B: The price freely negotiated between the divisions
options.C: Variable cost of the transferring division only
options.D: Cost of the transferring division plus an agreed mark-up

e: Under the cost-plus method, the transfer price is set at the cost of the transferring division plus an agreed mark-up representing its profit element.

q: When capital funds are limited (capital rationing), projects are generally ranked for selection on the basis of:

options.C: The Profitability Index, so that the net present value per rupee of the scarce capital is maximised
options.D: The initial cost of the project, lowest first

e: Under capital rationing, projects are ranked by the Profitability Index so that the maximum net present value is obtained per rupee of the scarce capital available.

q: A project's NPV is (+) Rs 4,000 at a discount rate of 10% and (-) Rs 2,000 at a discount rate of 12%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
A basic assumption of the IRR method, in contrast to the NPV method, is that the intermediate cash inflows of the project are reinvested at:

options.C: The internal rate of return itself
options.D: The bank rate

e: The IRR method assumes that intermediate cash inflows are reinvested at the internal rate of return itself, whereas the NPV method assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital.

q: Under the certainty-equivalent approach to risky projects, the expected cash flows are:

options.A: Discounted at a higher rate than usual
options.B: Multiplied by a certainty-equivalent coefficient (less than 1) to convert them into riskless equivalents, and then discounted at the risk-free rate
options.C: Ignored for the first year of the project
options.D: Increased by adding a risk premium to each inflow

e: Under the certainty-equivalent approach, expected cash flows are multiplied by a certainty-equivalent coefficient (less than 1) to convert them into riskless equivalents, which are then discounted at the risk-free rate.

q: Under the risk-adjusted discount rate approach, a riskier project is evaluated by:

options.A: Using the same discount rate as for a safe project
options.B: Discounting its cash flows at the risk-free rate only
options.C: Discounting its cash flows at a higher rate, which includes a risk premium over the normal rate
options.D: Extending its payback period by one year

e: Under the risk-adjusted discount rate approach, a riskier project's cash flows are discounted at a higher rate that includes a risk premium, reducing their present value.

q: A company has equity capital of Rs 6,00,000 with a cost of 15% and debt of Rs 4,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 9%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues debentures carrying interest at 12%. If the tax rate is 25%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so the after-tax cost of debt = 12% x (1 - 0.25) = 9%.

q: Retained earnings are not a cost-free source of finance because:

options.A: They carry an opportunity cost — the return the shareholders could have earned had the profits been distributed as dividends and invested elsewhere
options.B: Interest must be paid on them to the lenders
options.C: They must be repaid in cash at maturity
options.D: They are taxed at a special higher rate in the company's hands

e: Retained earnings carry an opportunity cost - the return shareholders could have earned had the profits been distributed as dividends and invested elsewhere - so they are not a cost-free source of finance.

q: The practice of using fixed-cost sources of finance, such as debt and preference capital, in the capital structure so as to magnify the returns to equity shareholders is known as:

options.D: Trading on equity (financial leverage)

e: Trading on equity (financial leverage) is the use of fixed-cost sources of finance such as debt and preference capital so as to magnify the returns to equity shareholders.

q: Under the Du Pont analysis, the Return on Investment is broken down into the product of:

options.A: The current ratio and the quick ratio
options.B: The debt-equity ratio and the interest coverage ratio
options.C: The gross profit ratio and the inventory turnover ratio
options.D: The net profit ratio and the capital (assets) turnover ratio

e: Under Du Pont analysis, ROI = Net profit ratio x Capital (assets) turnover ratio, breaking the return into a margin component and an asset-utilisation component.

q: An increase in the average collection period of debtors, other things being equal, indicates that:

options.A: Larger funds are blocked in receivables and realisation from debtors has become relatively lax
options.B: Credit control has become more efficient
options.D: The liquidity of the enterprise has improved

e: An increase in the average collection period means larger funds are blocked in receivables and realisation from debtors has become relatively lax, which worsens liquidity.

q: 'Common costs' are costs which:

options.A: Are incurred exclusively for one product
options.C: Are incurred for the common benefit of two or more cost objects and have to be apportioned among them on an equitable basis
options.D: Arise only when two products emerge from a single process

e: Common costs are incurred for the common benefit of two or more cost objects and have to be apportioned among them on an equitable basis; they are not confined to one product.

q: The Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) of a project indicates:

options.A: The ability of the project's earnings to cover its debt-service obligations, namely interest and repayment of principal
options.B: The proportion of debt in the total capital of the project
options.C: The rate of interest charged by the lenders
options.D: The dividend payable to the shareholders

e: The Debt Service Coverage Ratio indicates the ability of a project's earnings (cash flows) to cover its debt-service obligations, namely interest and repayment of principal.

q: Scenario analysis differs from sensitivity analysis in that scenario analysis:

options.A: Considers only one variable at a time
options.C: Is used only for analysing cost variances
options.D: Examines the effect of simultaneous changes in a number of variables under different assumed scenarios

e: Scenario analysis examines the effect of simultaneous changes in a number of variables under different assumed scenarios, whereas sensitivity analysis changes only one variable at a time.

q: In a project network, a 'dummy activity' is an activity which:

options.A: Consumes no time and no resources and is used only to show a precedence relationship
options.B: Is always performed by an outside contractor
options.C: Always lies on the critical path
options.D: Represents the final activity of the project

e: A dummy activity consumes no time and no resources and is used only to show a precedence relationship between events in a project network.

q: In preparing the financial justification of a railway project, the working expenses on the projected incremental traffic are commonly estimated by:

options.A: Ignoring them, since only capital cost matters
options.B: Charging them in full to the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.C: Taking the previous year's total working expenses of the whole railway
options.D: Applying the anticipated working-expenses (operating) ratio to the projected incremental earnings

e: In preparing financial justification, working expenses on the projected incremental traffic are commonly estimated by applying the anticipated working-expenses (operating) ratio to the projected incremental earnings.

q: A shortcoming frequently observed in the financial appraisal of railway projects is that:

options.A: Traffic and earnings tend to be over-estimated and costs under-estimated, so that the actual return falls short of the projected return
options.B: The DCF technique is never applied to any project
options.C: Projects are appraised only after they are completed
options.D: No rate of return is computed at the appraisal stage

e: A shortcoming frequently observed is that traffic and earnings tend to be over-estimated and costs under-estimated at the appraisal stage, so the actual return falls short of the projected return.

q: Under the Government's dividend guidelines for Central Public Sector Enterprises, a CPSE is expected to pay a minimum annual dividend of:

options.B: 30% of Profit After Tax or 4% of net worth, whichever is higher
options.D: 20% of Profit After Tax or 2% of net worth, whichever is higher

e: A CPSE is now expected to pay a minimum annual dividend of 30% of Profit After Tax or 4% of net worth, whichever is higher. (Source: DIPAM, Ministry of Finance, OM - Revised Guidelines on Capital Restructuring of CPSEs dated 18.11.2024; applicable from FY 2024-25.)

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 1,80,000 on sales of Rs 12,00,000. The net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = Net profit / Sales x 100 = 1,80,000 / 12,00,000 x 100 = 15%.

q: Prime cost of a product consists of:

options.B: Direct material, direct labour and direct expenses
options.D: Total factory cost less work-in-progress

e: Prime cost is the total of all direct costs of production - direct material consumed, direct labour and direct (chargeable) expenses. Overheads of any kind are excluded at this stage.

q: When the level of output increases, the fixed cost per unit:

options.A: Decreases, because the total fixed cost remains unchanged and is spread over more units
options.B: Increases in the same proportion as output
options.C: Remains constant per unit at all levels of output
options.D: Decreases because the total fixed cost itself falls

e: Total fixed cost does not change with output, so when it is spread over a larger number of units the fixed cost per unit falls. The variable cost per unit, by contrast, stays constant.

q: The total cost of producing 8,000 units is Rs 52,000 and that of producing 12,000 units is Rs 68,000. Using the high-low method, the fixed cost is:
Interest on the proprietor's own capital and rent of premises owned by the firm, for which no cash is actually paid, are examples of:

options.D: Imputed (notional) costs

e: Imputed or notional costs involve no actual cash outlay but are considered in cost accounts for decision-making and comparison, e.g. interest on own capital and rent of own premises.

q: ABC analysis for selective control of inventory classifies items into A, B and C categories primarily on the basis of:

options.A: The physical size of the items
options.B: The annual consumption value of the items
options.C: The lead time for procurement of the items
options.D: The storage space occupied by the items

e: ABC analysis ranks inventory items by their annual consumption value (annual usage x unit price). High-value A items get tight control, moderate-value B items less, and low-value C items only simple control.

q: The maximum usage of a material is 400 units per week and the maximum lead time is 5 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:

options.D: 800 units

e: Re-order level = maximum usage x maximum lead time = 400 units per week x 5 weeks = 2,000 units, so that stock lasts even in the worst combination of usage and delay.

q: Which of the following methods of valuing inventory is NOT permitted under Ind AS 2?

options.D: Specific identification for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable

e: Ind AS 2 permits FIFO and weighted average cost (and specific identification for non-interchangeable items), but prohibits LIFO because it can leave old, unrealistic costs in the closing inventory.

q: A bin card maintained in the stores:

options.A: Records both quantities and values of materials
options.B: Is maintained by the cost accounts department
options.C: Serves the same purpose as the stores ledger
options.D: Records only quantities — receipts, issues and balance — of each item of material

e: A bin card, kept by the storekeeper at the bin, is a purely quantitative record of receipts, issues and running balance of each item. Values are recorded only in the stores ledger.

q: A worker is allowed 10 hours for a job and completes it in 8 hours at a wage rate of Rs 50 per hour. His total earnings under the Halsey premium bonus plan (50% of time saved) are:

options.D: Rs 480

e: Halsey plan: wages for time taken 8 hrs x Rs 50 = Rs 400, plus bonus of 50% of time saved (2 hrs x Rs 50 x 50%) = Rs 50. Total = Rs 450.

q: A worker is allowed 10 hours for a job and completes it in 8 hours at a wage rate of Rs 50 per hour. His total earnings under the Rowan premium bonus plan are:

options.D: Rs 500

e: Rowan plan: time wages 8 hrs x Rs 50 = Rs 400, plus bonus = (time saved / time allowed) x time taken x rate = (2/10) x 8 x 50 = Rs 80. Total = Rs 480.

q: Wages paid for abnormal idle time, such as time lost due to a major power failure or a machine breakdown, are:

options.A: Included in the direct wages of the job in hand
options.C: Charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account and excluded from the cost of production
options.D: Recovered from the workers responsible for the stoppage

e: Abnormal idle time is uncontrollable and not a normal cost of production, so its wages are excluded from product cost and charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: During a year, 45 workers left a factory whose average number of workers on roll was 900. The labour turnover rate (separation method) is:
e: Labour turnover (separation method) = workers left / average workers on roll x 100 = 45 / 900 x 100 = 5%.

q: Budgeted factory overheads are Rs 2,40,000 and budgeted machine hours are 48,000. Actual machine hours worked are 46,000 and actual overheads incurred are Rs 2,44,000. The overheads are:

options.D: Over-absorbed by Rs 4,000

e: Overhead rate = 2,40,000 / 48,000 = Rs 5 per machine hour. Absorbed = 46,000 x 5 = Rs 2,30,000 against actual Rs 2,44,000, so overheads are under-absorbed by Rs 14,000.

q: In overhead analysis, 'secondary distribution' means:

options.A: Apportionment of the overhead costs of service cost centres to production cost centres
options.B: Absorption of overheads into the cost of products
options.C: Distribution of factory overheads among all departments in the first stage
options.D: Charging of overheads to the profit and loss account

e: After primary distribution of overheads to all cost centres, secondary distribution re-apportions the total cost of service cost centres (stores, maintenance, etc.) to production cost centres, which alone produce output.

q: In computing the machine hour rate, which of the following is a standing (fixed) charge relating to the machine?

options.B: Consumable stores used in running the machine
options.D: Repairs varying with the hours run

e: Standing charges are fixed machine costs that do not vary with running hours, such as insurance premium, rent and rates. Power, consumable stores and running repairs vary with use and are machine expenses.

q: Under marginal costing, the closing stock of finished goods is valued at:

options.A: Total cost including fixed production overheads
options.B: Cost of production plus selling overheads
options.D: Marginal (variable) cost of production only

e: Under marginal costing, only variable production cost is treated as product cost, so closing stock carries marginal cost alone. Fixed production overheads are written off as period costs.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 60,000. Production during the period is 12,000 units and sales are 10,000 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing will be:

options.D: Exactly the same

e: Fixed overhead rate = 60,000 / 12,000 = Rs 5 per unit. Stock rises by 2,000 units, so absorption costing defers 2,000 x Rs 5 = Rs 10,000 of fixed cost in stock, giving Rs 10,000 higher profit.

q: Under the marginal costing technique, fixed production overheads are treated as:

options.A: Period costs, charged in full against the profit of the period in which they are incurred
options.B: Product costs, carried forward in the value of closing stock
options.C: A part of the marginal cost of each unit produced
options.D: Deferred costs to be matched with future sales

e: Fixed production overheads do not vary with output and are regarded as costs of the period under marginal costing; they are charged wholly against the contribution of the period incurred.

q: If production is exactly equal to sales during a period, so that stock levels do not change, then:

options.A: Profit under absorption costing is always higher
options.B: Profit under marginal costing is always higher
options.C: The profit shown by absorption costing and by marginal costing is the same
options.D: No profit can be computed under marginal costing

e: The only difference between the two profits arises from fixed overhead carried in opening and closing stock. If production equals sales, stock is unchanged, so both methods report identical profit.

q: A product sells for Rs 60 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 36 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 1,44,000. The break-even point in units is:

options.D: 6,000 units

e: Contribution per unit = 60 - 36 = Rs 24. Break-even units = fixed cost / contribution per unit = 1,44,000 / 24 = 6,000 units.

q: A product sells for Rs 200 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 140 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 1,80,000. The number of units to be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 1,20,000 is:

options.D: 7,500 units

e: Contribution per unit = 200 - 140 = Rs 60. Units needed = (fixed cost + target profit) / 60 = (1,80,000 + 1,20,000) / 60 = 5,000 units.

q: An enterprise wants to earn a profit after tax of Rs 72,000. The tax rate is 25%, fixed costs are Rs 1,44,000 and the P/V ratio is 40%. The sales required are:
e: Profit before tax needed = 72,000 / (1 - 0.25) = Rs 96,000. Sales = (fixed cost + profit before tax) / P/V ratio = (1,44,000 + 96,000) / 40% = Rs 6,00,000.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 6,00,000, its P/V ratio is 30% and fixed costs are Rs 1,20,000. Its profit is:
e: Contribution = sales x P/V ratio = 6,00,000 x 30% = Rs 1,80,000. Profit = contribution - fixed cost = 1,80,000 - 1,20,000 = Rs 60,000.

q: The total sales of a firm are Rs 10,00,000 and its margin of safety is 40% of total sales. Its break-even sales are:
e: Margin of safety is the excess of actual sales over break-even sales. Break-even sales = total sales x (1 - 40%) = 10,00,000 x 60% = Rs 6,00,000.

q: A firm sells two products: P with sales of Rs 3,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 40%, and Q with sales of Rs 2,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 30%. Total fixed costs are Rs 1,44,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
e: Total contribution = (3,00,000 x 40%) + (2,00,000 x 30%) = Rs 1,80,000 on sales of Rs 5,00,000, so overall P/V ratio = 36%. Break-even sales = 1,44,000 / 36% = Rs 4,00,000.

q: Machine hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 40 per unit and requires 2 machine hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 75 per unit and requires 5 machine hours per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per machine hour (Rs 20) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Product B, because it keeps the machines engaged for longer
options.D: Both products in equal proportion

e: With a scarce resource, products are ranked by contribution per unit of the limiting factor. A gives 40/2 = Rs 20 per machine hour against B's 75/5 = Rs 15, so A gets priority.

q: A factory has 10,000 machine hours available. Product A requires 4 hours per unit, gives a contribution of Rs 120 per unit and its maximum demand is 1,500 units. Product B requires 2 hours per unit and gives a contribution of Rs 44 per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:

options.D: 2,500 units

e: A uses 1,500 x 4 = 6,000 of the 10,000 hours. Remaining 4,000 hours at 2 hours per unit of B give 4,000 / 2 = 2,000 units of B.

q: A component can be made in the factory at a variable cost of Rs 45 per unit, or bought from outside at Rs 50 per unit. If the component is bought, the released capacity can be used to earn a contribution of Rs 6 per unit on other work. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make, because the variable cost of making is less than the purchase price
options.B: Buy, because the effective cost of buying (Rs 50 − Rs 6 = Rs 44) is less than the cost of making it
options.C: Make, because outside supply is always unreliable
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the net difference is nil

e: The effective cost of buying is the price minus the contribution the freed capacity can earn: 50 - 6 = Rs 44 per unit, which is less than the Rs 45 cost of making, so buying is better.

q: A firm with spare capacity receives a one-time special order for 5,000 units at Rs 80 per unit. The variable cost is Rs 70 per unit, but accepting the order requires special tooling costing Rs 30,000. The order should be:

options.A: Rejected, because the special tooling cost makes it unprofitable
options.B: Accepted only if the price is raised to Rs 90 per unit
options.C: Rejected, because the price is below the normal selling price
options.D: Accepted, because it yields a net incremental gain of Rs 20,000

e: Incremental gain = contribution on the order minus the extra tooling cost = 5,000 x (80 - 70) - 30,000 = 50,000 - 30,000 = Rs 20,000. With spare capacity, the order is worth accepting.

q: A division has sales of Rs 1,00,000, variable costs of Rs 70,000 and specific (avoidable) fixed costs of Rs 25,000; allocated common fixed costs are Rs 20,000. If the division is closed down, the total profit of the company will:

options.D: Remain unchanged

e: The division's segment margin = 1,00,000 - 70,000 - 25,000 = Rs 5,000 positive. Closure loses this margin while the allocated common costs continue, so company profit falls by Rs 5,000.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 2,00,000 per year, of which Rs 60,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. The contribution is Rs 28 per unit. The shutdown point is:

options.D: 10,000 units

e: Shutdown point = (total fixed cost - shutdown fixed cost) / contribution per unit = (2,00,000 - 60,000) / 28 = 5,000 units; below this output, shutting down loses less.

q: For actual output, the standard material cost is 1,000 kg at Rs 10 per kg. The actual consumption is 1,100 kg at Rs 11 per kg. The material cost variance is:

options.D: Rs 1,100 (Adverse)

e: Material cost variance = standard cost - actual cost = (1,000 x 10) - (1,100 x 11) = 10,000 - 12,100 = Rs 2,100 adverse.

q: For actual output, the standard labour cost is 2,000 hours at Rs 50 per hour. Actual hours worked are 2,100 at Rs 52 per hour. The labour cost variance is:

options.D: Rs 9,200 (Adverse)

e: Labour cost variance = standard cost - actual cost = (2,000 x 50) - (2,100 x 52) = 1,00,000 - 1,09,200 = Rs 9,200 adverse.

q: In a factory, 50 hours were lost as abnormal idle time. The standard wage rate is Rs 40 per hour. The idle time variance is:

options.D: Nil

e: Idle time variance = idle hours x standard rate = 50 x Rs 40 = Rs 2,000, always adverse because paid hours produced no output.

q: The standard mix for a batch of 100 kg is: Material X — 60 kg at Rs 10 per kg, Material Y — 40 kg at Rs 20 per kg. The actual mix used for a 100 kg batch is X — 70 kg and Y — 30 kg. The material mix variance is:

options.D: Rs 200 (Adverse)

e: Mix variance at standard prices: standard mix cost = (60 x 10) + (40 x 20) = Rs 1,400; actual mix = (70 x 10) + (30 x 20) = Rs 1,300. Using more of cheaper X gives Rs 100 favourable.

q: A process has a standard yield of 80 kg of output from 100 kg of input, the input costing Rs 40 per kg. The actual output obtained from 100 kg of input is 75 kg. The material yield variance is:

options.D: Rs 125 (Adverse)

e: Standard cost per kg of output = (100 x 40) / 80 = Rs 50. The yield shortfall of 5 kg (80 - 75) x Rs 50 = Rs 250 adverse.

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 10,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 4 per unit. Actual production is 9,000 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:

options.D: Rs 4,000 (Adverse)

e: Volume variance = (actual production - budgeted production) x standard rate = (9,000 - 10,000) x Rs 4 = Rs 4,000 adverse, as fixed overhead is under-absorbed on lower output.

q: In a process, 1,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 19,800. Normal loss is 10% of input and the scrap realises Rs 18 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Normal loss = 100 units; scrap value = 100 x 18 = Rs 1,800. Cost of good output = (19,800 - 1,800) / 900 good units = Rs 20.00 per unit.

q: In process costing, an abnormal loss is valued:

options.A: At the scrap value of the units only
options.B: At the selling price of the finished product
options.C: At the same cost per unit as good output, and the net loss (after scrap recovery) is transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: It is ignored in the cost accounts

e: Abnormal loss units are valued at the full cost per unit of good output, like normal production. After deducting any scrap recovered, the net loss is written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: A joint cost of Rs 1,60,000 is to be apportioned between Products A and B on the basis of their sales values at the split-off point: A — Rs 3,00,000 and B — Rs 1,00,000. The share of joint cost borne by Product A is:
e: Apportionment in the sales-value ratio 3,00,000 : 1,00,000, i.e. 3:1. A's share = 1,60,000 x 3/4 = Rs 1,20,000.

q: Operating (service) costing is applied by undertakings such as:

options.D: Transport companies, hospitals and hotels rendering services

e: Operating costing is used where a standardised service is rendered rather than goods produced, e.g. transport, hospitals, hotels and canteens, with cost units like the passenger-kilometre or bed-day.

q: In transport costing, which of the following is a standing charge?

options.A: Licence fee and insurance premium of the vehicle
options.C: Wear and tear of tyres varying with the distance run
options.D: Repairs varying with the kilometres run

e: Standing charges in transport costing are fixed costs incurred whether the vehicle runs or not, such as licence fee, insurance, garage rent and the driver's fixed salary. Fuel and running repairs vary with distance.

q: A transport undertaking incurs a total operating cost of Rs 4,80,000 during a period in which its effective passenger-kilometres are 24,00,000. The cost per passenger-kilometre is:
e: Cost per passenger-kilometre = total operating cost / effective passenger-kilometres = 4,80,000 / 24,00,000 = Rs 0.20.

q: Under activity-based costing, for the procurement (buying) activity of a factory, the most appropriate cost driver is:

options.A: The floor area of the stores
options.B: The number of purchase orders placed
options.C: The direct labour hours of production workers
options.D: The value of finished goods sold

e: ABC assigns activity costs through cost drivers that cause the activity. Procurement cost is driven by the number of purchase orders placed, not by labour hours or floor area.

q: Under activity-based costing, the set-up cost pool of a plant is Rs 3,00,000 and the total number of set-ups in the period is 150. A product requiring 25 set-ups will be assigned set-up cost of:
e: Set-up cost rate = 3,00,000 / 150 set-ups = Rs 2,000 per set-up. Cost assigned to the product = 25 x 2,000 = Rs 50,000.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 2,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 1,00,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 3 years at 10% is 2.487. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: Present value of inflows = 1,00,000 x 2.487 = Rs 2,48,700. NPV = 2,48,700 - 2,00,000 = (+) Rs 48,700, so the project is acceptable.

q: A project costing Rs 2,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 90,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 90,000 at the end of Year 2, besides a salvage value of Rs 20,000 at the end of Year 2. The present value factors at 10% are 0.909 for Year 1 and 0.826 for Year 2. The Net Present Value of the project is:

A project with an initial outlay of Rs 2,80,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 12% = 0.893) and Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 12% = 0.797). Its Net Present Value is:
The present value of Rs 1,00,000 receivable at the end of 2 years, discounted at 10% (present value factor 0.826), is:
e: Present value = future amount x present value factor = 1,00,000 x 0.826 = Rs 82,600.

q: Rs 1,00,000 invested today at 10% per annum compound interest will grow in 2 years to:
